label: Definition 8.1
Definition 8.2
Lemma 8.1
Lemma 8.2
Lemma 8.3
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:lem:8.3}
For $n\ge 1$ and $x\in\Omega$, define
\[
\label{eq:8.u10}
f_n(x):=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{k}{2^n}, & \text{if } \dfrac{k}{2^n}\le f(x)<\dfrac{k+1}{2^n}\text{ for some integer }k\in\{0,1,\dots,n2^n-1\},\\
n, & \text{if } f(x)\ge n.
\end{cases}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\label{eq:8.u11}
f_n(x)=\min\Bigl(n,\frac{\lfloor 2^n f(x)\rfloor}{2^n}\Bigr),
\]
with the convention that $\lfloor 2^n f(x)\rfloor=+\infty$ when $f(x)=+\infty$.

Each $f_n$ takes values in the finite set $\{0,2^{-n},2\cdot 2^{-n},\dots,n\}$, hence is simple. To see measurability, it suffices to check that for each $a\in\mathbb{R}$ the set $\{x\in\Omega: f_n(x)>a\}$ is measurable. Using the explicit definition above, one can write $\{f_n>a\}$ as a finite union of sets of the form $\{f\ge n\}$ and $\{\frac{k}{2^n}\le f<\frac{k+1}{2^n}\}$, each of which is measurable because $f$ is measurable. Thus $f_n$ is measurable. Nonnegativity is immediate.

For monotonicity, fix $x\in\Omega$ and set $t=f(x)\in[0,+\infty]$. If $t\ge n+1$, then $f_n(x)=n\le n+1=f_{n+1}(x)$. If $t<n+1$, then
\[
\label{eq:8.u12}
f_n(x)=\min\Bigl(n,\frac{\lfloor 2^n t\rfloor}{2^n}\Bigr)\le \min\Bigl(n+1,\frac{\lfloor 2^{n+1} t\rfloor}{2^{n+1}}\Bigr)=f_{n+1}(x),
\]
since $\lfloor 2^n t\rfloor/2^n\le \lfloor 2^{n+1} t\rfloor/2^{n+1}$.

Finally, for pointwise convergence, fix $x\in\Omega$.
If $f(x)=+\infty$, then for every $n$ one has $f_n(x)=n$, hence $f_n(x)\to+\infty=f(x)$.
If $f(x)=t<+\infty$, then for all $n>t$ one has $f_n(x)=\lfloor 2^n t\rfloor/2^n$ and therefore
\[
\label{eq:8.u13}
0\le t-f_n(x)=t-\frac{\lfloor 2^n t\rfloor}{2^n}<\frac{1}{2^n},
\]
which implies $f_n(x)\to t=f(x)$ as $n\to\infty$.
\end{proof}

label: Definition 8.3

Proposition 8.1.1

Definition 8.4
Proposition 8.2
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:8.2}
Assume first that $f(x)=0$ for $\mu$-almost every $x\in\Omega$. Then there exists $N\in\Sigma$ with $\mu(N)=0$ such that $f=0$ on $\Omega\setminus N$. Hence $f\,\mathbf{1}_{\Omega\setminus N}=0$ and $f\,\mathbf{1}_N\ge 0$, so by monotonicity of the integral,
\[
\label{eq:8.u27}
0\le \int_\Omega f\,d\mu=\int_{\Omega\setminus N} f\,d\mu+\int_N f\,d\mu=0+\int_N f\,d\mu\le \int_N \infty\,d\mu=0,
\]
which gives $\int_\Omega f\,d\mu=0$.

Conversely, assume $\int_\Omega f\,d\mu=0$. For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ define
\[
\label{eq:8.u28}
A_n:=\{x\in\Omega: f(x)\ge 1/n\}\in\Sigma.
\]
Then $f\ge \frac1n\mathbf{1}_{A_n}$, and by monotonicity of the integral,
\[
\label{eq:8.u29}
0=\int_\Omega f\,d\mu\ge \int_\Omega \frac1n\mathbf{1}_{A_n}\,d\mu=\frac1n\mu(A_n).
\]
Hence $\mu(A_n)=0$ for all $n$. If $B:=\{x\in\Omega: f(x)>0\}$, then $B=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n$, so
\[
\label{eq:8.u30}
\mu(B)\le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu(A_n)=0.
\]
Therefore $\mu(\{f>0\})=0$, equivalently $f(x)=0$ for $\mu$-almost every $x\in\Omega$.
\end{proof}

label: Definition 8.5
Definition 8.6
Proposition 8.3.1

Theorem 8.1
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:8.1}
For each $n$, the inequality $f_n\le f_{n+1}$ implies $\int_\Omega f_n\le \int_\Omega f_{n+1}$ by monotonicity of the Lebesgue integral for nonnegative measurable functions.

Let $f=\sup_{m\ge1} f_m$. Since $f\ge f_n$ pointwise for every $n$, monotonicity also gives
\[
\label{eq:8.u40}
\int_\Omega f\ge \int_\Omega f_n\quad\text{for all }n,
\]
hence
\[
\label{eq:8.u41}
\int_\Omega f\ge \sup_{n\ge1}\int_\Omega f_n.
\]

To prove the reverse inequality, it suffices (by definition of the integral of a nonnegative measurable function as the supremum of integrals of simple minorants) to show that for every simple function $s:\Omega\to[0,+\infty)$ with $s\le f$ pointwise,
\[
\label{eq:8.u42}
\int_\Omega s\le \sup_{n\ge1}\int_\Omega f_n.
\]
Fix such an $s$ and fix $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$. For each $n$ define
\[
\label{eq:8.u43}
E_n:=\{x\in\Omega: f_n(x)\ge (1-\varepsilon)s(x)\}.
\]
Each $E_n$ is measurable, $(E_n)$ is increasing, and $\bigcup_{n\ge1}E_n=\Omega$: indeed, for each $x\in\Omega$, the inequality $s(x)\le \sup_m f_m(x)$ implies the existence of $N$ with $f_N(x)\ge (1-\varepsilon)s(x)$, and then $x\in E_n$ for all $n\ge N$ since $(f_n)$ is increasing.

On $E_n$ one has $(1-\varepsilon)s\le f_n$, so monotonicity yields
\[
\label{eq:8.u44}
(1-\varepsilon)\int_{E_n} s\le \int_{E_n} f_n\le \int_\Omega f_n\le \sup_{k\ge1}\int_\Omega f_k.
\]
Taking the supremum over $n$ gives
\[
\label{eq:8.u45}
(1-\varepsilon)\sup_{n\ge1}\int_{E_n} s\le \sup_{k\ge1}\int_\Omega f_k.
\]
It remains to compute $\sup_n\int_{E_n} s$. Write $s=\sum_{j=1}^N c_j\chi_{F_j}$ with $c_j>0$ and measurable $F_j$. Then
\[
\label{eq:8.u46}
\int_{E_n} s=\sum_{j=1}^N c_j\,m(F_j\cap E_n).
\]
For each fixed $j$, the sets $F_j\cap E_n$ increase to $F_j$ because $E_n\uparrow\Omega$, hence by continuity from below of Lebesgue measure,
\[
\label{eq:8.u47}
\sup_{n\ge1} m(F_j\cap E_n)=\lim_{n\to\infty} m(F_j\cap E_n)=m(F_j).
\]
Therefore
\[
\label{eq:8.u48}
\sup_{n\ge1}\int_{E_n} s=\sum_{j=1}^N c_j\,\sup_{n\ge1}m(F_j\cap E_n)=\sum_{j=1}^N c_j m(F_j)=\int_\Omega s.
\]
Combining with the previous inequality yields
\[
\label{eq:8.u49}
(1-\varepsilon)\int_\Omega s\le \sup_{k\ge1}\int_\Omega f_k.
\]
Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ gives $\int_\Omega s\le \sup_k\int_\Omega f_k$. Taking the supremum over all simple $s\le f$ yields $\int_\Omega f\le \sup_k\int_\Omega f_k$, completing the proof.
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 8.5
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:lem:8.5}
There exist sequences of simple functions $(s_k)_{k\ge 1}$ and $(t_k)_{k\ge 1}$ such that $0\le s_1\le s_2\le\cdots$ and $\sup_k s_k=f$, and $0\le t_1\le t_2\le\cdots$ and $\sup_k t_k=g$ (pointwise on $\Omega$). Then $(s_k+t_k)_{k\ge 1}$ is an increasing sequence of simple functions and
\[
\label{eq:8.u51}
\sup_k (s_k+t_k)=\sup_k s_k+\sup_k t_k=f+g.
\]
By the monotone convergence theorem,
\[
\label{eq:8.u52}
\int_{\Omega} f=\sup_k\int_{\Omega} s_k,\qquad \int_{\Omega} g=\sup_k\int_{\Omega} t_k,\qquad \int_{\Omega} (f+g)=\sup_k\int_{\Omega} (s_k+t_k).
\]
For each $k$, additivity of the integral for simple functions gives
\[
\label{eq:8.u53}
\int_{\Omega} (s_k+t_k)=\int_{\Omega} s_k+\int_{\Omega} t_k.
\]
Since $\int_{\Omega} s_k$ and $\int_{\Omega} t_k$ are increasing in $k$,
\[
\label{eq:8.u54}
\sup_k\left(\int_{\Omega} s_k+\int_{\Omega} t_k\right)=\left(\sup_k\int_{\Omega} s_k\right)+\left(\sup_k\int_{\Omega} t_k\right).
\]
Combining these equalities yields
\[
\label{eq:8.u55}
\int_{\Omega} (f+g)=\int_{\Omega} f+\int_{\Omega} g.
\]
\end{proof}

label: Theorem 8.2
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:8.2}
For $N\ge 1$ define the partial sums
\[
\label{eq:8.u58}
G_N(x):=\sum_{n=1}^{N} g_n(x),\qquad x\in\Omega.
\]
Each $G_N$ is measurable as a finite sum of measurable functions, and $(G_N)_{N\ge 1}$ is pointwise non-decreasing with
\[
\label{eq:8.u59}
G_N(x)\uparrow G(x)\quad\text{for all }x\in\Omega.
\]
Since $G=\sup_{N\ge 1} G_N$, the function $G$ is measurable.

By the monotone convergence theorem applied to $G_N\uparrow G$,
\[
\label{eq:8.u60}
\int_{\Omega} G\,=\,\lim_{N\to\infty}\int_{\Omega} G_N.
\]
For each $N$,
\[
\label{eq:8.u61}
\int_{\Omega} G_N=\int_{\Omega}\sum_{n=1}^{N} g_n=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\int_{\Omega} g_n,
\]
by linearity of the integral for non-negative measurable functions and finite sums. Taking limits as $N\to\infty$ yields
\[
\label{eq:8.u62}
\int_{\Omega} G=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\int_{\Omega} g_n=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega} g_n.
\]
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 8.6
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:lem:8.6}
For each $n\ge 1$ define
\[
\label{eq:8.u64}
g_n(x):=\inf_{m\ge n} f_m(x),\qquad x\in\Omega.
\]
Then each $g_n$ is measurable, $0\le g_n\le g_{n+1}$ pointwise, and
\[
\label{eq:8.u65}
\lim_{n\to\infty} g_n(x)=\sup_{n\ge 1} g_n(x)=\sup_{n\ge 1}\inf_{m\ge n} f_m(x)=\liminf_{n\to\infty} f_n(x).
\]
By the monotone convergence theorem,
\[
\label{eq:8.u66}
\int_{\Omega} \liminf_{n\to\infty} f_n\,dx
=\int_{\Omega} \lim_{n\to\infty} g_n\,dx
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{\Omega} g_n\,dx
=\sup_{n\ge 1}\int_{\Omega} g_n\,dx.
\]
For fixed $n$ and any $j\ge n$, the pointwise inequality $g_n\le f_j$ implies
\[
\label{eq:8.u67}
\int_{\Omega} g_n\,dx\le \int_{\Omega} f_j\,dx.
\]
Taking the infimum over $j\ge n$ yields
\[
\label{eq:8.u68}
\int_{\Omega} g_n\,dx\le \inf_{j\ge n}\int_{\Omega} f_j\,dx.
\]
Taking the supremum over $n$ gives
\[
\label{eq:8.u69}
\int_{\Omega} \liminf_{n\to\infty} f_n\,dx
=\sup_{n\ge 1}\int_{\Omega} g_n\,dx
\le \sup_{n\ge 1}\inf_{j\ge n}\int_{\Omega} f_j\,dx
=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_{\Omega} f_n\,dx.
\]
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 8.4
Lemma 8.7
Lemma 8.8
Proposition 8.5
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:8.5}
If $\int_{\Omega} f=+\infty$ or $\int_{\Omega} g=+\infty$, then $\int_{\Omega}(f+g)=+\infty$ because $f+g\ge f$ and $f+g\ge g$, so the inequality holds.

Assume $\int_{\Omega} f<+\infty$ and $\int_{\Omega} g<+\infty$. For $k\in\mathbb{N}$ define the truncated functions
\[
\label{eq:8.u80}
f_k:=\min\{f,k\},\qquad g_k:=\min\{g,k\}.
\]
Then $f_k,g_k$ are measurable, nonnegative, and bounded. Moreover $f_k\uparrow f$ and $g_k\uparrow g$ pointwise, and also $f_k+g_k\uparrow f+g$ pointwise.

Since $f_k,g_k$ are bounded and nonnegative, they are integrable and satisfy additivity of the integral:
\[
\label{eq:8.u81}
\int_{\Omega}(f_k+g_k)=\int_{\Omega} f_k+\int_{\Omega} g_k.
\]
By the monotone convergence theorem,
\[
\label{eq:8.u82}
\int_{\Omega}(f+g)=\lim_{k\to\infty}\int_{\Omega}(f_k+g_k)=\lim_{k\to\infty}\left(\int_{\Omega} f_k+\int_{\Omega} g_k\right)=\int_{\Omega} f+\int_{\Omega} g.
\]
In particular, $\int_{\Omega}(f+g)\ge \int_{\Omega} f+\int_{\Omega} g$.
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 8.6
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:8.6}
For each integer $q\ge 1$ define
\[
\label{eq:8.u84}
E_q:=\bigcup_{a=1}^q \left( \left[\frac{a}{q}-\frac{c}{q^p},\,\frac{a}{q}+\frac{c}{q^p}\right]\cap[0,1]\right).
\]
If $x\in E$, then $x\in E_q$ for infinitely many $q$, so
\[
\label{eq:8.u85}
E\subseteq \limsup_{q\to\infty} E_q:=\bigcap_{N=1}^\infty\bigcup_{q\ge N} E_q.
\]
Let $m$ denote Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$. For each $q$, the set $E_q$ is a union of at most $q$ intervals, each of length at most $\frac{2c}{q^p}$; hence
\[
\label{eq:8.u86}
m(E_q)\le q\cdot \frac{2c}{q^p}=\frac{2c}{q^{p-1}}.
\]
Fix $N\ge 1$. By subadditivity,
\[
\label{eq:8.u87}
m\Bigl(\bigcup_{q\ge N} E_q\Bigr)\le \sum_{q=N}^\infty m(E_q)\le \sum_{q=N}^\infty \frac{2c}{q^{p-1}}.
\]
Since $p-1>1$, the series $\sum_{q=1}^\infty q^{-(p-1)}$ converges, so the tail $\sum_{q=N}^\infty \frac{2c}{q^{p-1}}\to 0$ as $N\to\infty$. Therefore
\[
\label{eq:8.u88}
m\Bigl(\limsup_{q\to\infty} E_q\Bigr)\le \inf_{N\ge 1} m\Bigl(\bigcup_{q\ge N} E_q\Bigr)=0.
\]
Because $E\subseteq \limsup_{q\to\infty}E_q$, it follows that $m(E)=0$.
\end{proof}

label: Definition 8.7
Theorem 8.3
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:8.3}
Fix $\tau>2$. For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ define
\[
\label{eq:8.u92}
E_n:=\bigcup_{q=1}^\infty\ \bigcup_{p\in\mathbb{Z}} \left(\frac{p}{q}-\frac{1}{n q^{\tau}},\ \frac{p}{q}+\frac{1}{n q^{\tau}}\right).
\]
Then $x\in E_n$ if and only if there exist infinitely many pairs $(p,q)\in\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{N}$ such that $\left|x-\frac{p}{q}\right|<\frac{1}{n q^{\tau}}$. Hence the complement
\[
\label{eq:8.u93}
D_\tau:=\mathbb{R}\setminus\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty E_n
\]
consists exactly of those $x$ for which there exists $n$ (equivalently $c=1/n$) such that $\left|x-\frac{p}{q}\right|\ge \frac{1}{n q^{\tau}}$ for all $p,q$, i.e. the diophantine numbers of exponent $\tau$.

To show that $D_\tau$ has full Lebesgue measure it suffices to prove that each $E_n$ has Lebesgue measure zero.

Fix $n$. By translation invariance it is enough to estimate $m(E_n\cap[0,1])$, where $m$ denotes Lebesgue measure. For each $q\ge 1$, the rationals $p/q$ with $0\le p\le q$ cover all possible centers in $[0,1]$ (up to endpoints), and for fixed $q$ the union of intervals
\[
\label{eq:8.u94}
\bigcup_{p=0}^q \left(\frac{p}{q}-\frac{1}{n q^{\tau}},\ \frac{p}{q}+\frac{1}{n q^{\tau}}\right)
\]
has total length at most $(q+1)\cdot \frac{2}{n q^{\tau}}$. Therefore
\[
\label{eq:8.u95}
m(E_n\cap[0,1])\le \sum_{q=1}^\infty (q+1)\frac{2}{n q^{\tau}}
\le \frac{4}{n}\sum_{q=1}^\infty \frac{1}{q^{\tau-1}}.
\]
Since $\tau>2$, the series $\sum_{q\ge1} q^{-(\tau-1)}$ converges. Apply the Borel--Cantelli lemma to the events
\[
\label{eq:8.u96}
A_{q}:=\bigcup_{p\in\mathbb{Z}} \left(\frac{p}{q}-\frac{1}{n q^{\tau}},\ \frac{p}{q}+\frac{1}{n q^{\tau}}\right)\cap[0,1],
\]
noting that $m(A_q)\le \frac{2(q+1)}{n q^{\tau}}\le \frac{4}{n q^{\tau-1}}$ and that $\sum_{q\ge1} m(A_q)<\infty$ whenever $\tau>2$. Thus for almost every $x\in[0,1]$ there exists $c(x)>0$ such that $\left|x-\frac{p}{q}\right|\ge \frac{c(x)}{q^{\tau}}$ for all $p,q$. By translation invariance the same holds on $\mathbb{R}$, so the set of diophantine numbers of exponent $\tau$ has full Lebesgue measure.
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 8.7
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:8.7}
Fix $\varepsilon>0$. For each $n\ge 1$ define
\[
\label{eq:8.u102}
A_n:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}: f_n(x)>2^{-n}\}.
\]
By Markov's inequality,
\[
\label{eq:8.u103}
m(A_n)\le 2^n\int_{\mathbb{R}} f_n\,dm\le 2^n\cdot 4^{-n}=2^{-n}.
\]
Choose $N\ge 1$ such that $\sum_{n\ge N}2^{-n}\le \varepsilon$. Define
\[
\label{eq:8.u104}
E:=\bigcup_{n\ge N} A_n.
\]
Then $E$ is measurable and
\[
\label{eq:8.u105}
m(E)\le \sum_{n\ge N} m(A_n)\le \sum_{n\ge N}2^{-n}\le \varepsilon.
\]
If $x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus E$, then $x\notin A_n$ for every $n\ge N$, hence $f_n(x)\le 2^{-n}$ for all $n\ge N$. Therefore $f_n(x)\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus E$.
\end{proof}

label: Theorem 8.4
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:8.4}
Fix $\varepsilon>0$. For $k\in\mathbb N$ and $N\in\mathbb N$ define
\[
\label{eq:8.u106}
A_{k,N}:=\bigcup_{n\ge N}\{x\in[0,1]: f_n(x)>1/k\}.
\]
Each $A_{k,N}$ is measurable, and $A_{k,N+1}\subset A_{k,N}$. Since $f_n(x)\to 0$ for every $x$, for each fixed $k$ and each $x\in[0,1]$ there exists $N$ such that $f_n(x)\le 1/k$ for all $n\ge N$, hence $x\notin A_{k,N}$. Therefore
\[
\label{eq:8.u107}
\bigcap_{N=1}^\infty A_{k,N}=\varnothing.
\]
By continuity from above of Lebesgue measure on the finite-measure space $([0,1],m)$,
\[
\label{eq:8.u108}
\lim_{N\to\infty} m(A_{k,N})= m\Bigl(\bigcap_{N=1}^\infty A_{k,N}\Bigr)=0.
\]
For each $k\in\mathbb N$ choose $N_k\in\mathbb N$ such that $m(A_{k,N_k})\le \varepsilon 2^{-k}$. Set
\[
\label{eq:8.u109}
E:=\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty A_{k,N_k}.
\]
Then $E$ is measurable and
\[
\label{eq:8.u110}
m(E)\le \sum_{k=1}^\infty m(A_{k,N_k})\le \sum_{k=1}^\infty \varepsilon 2^{-k}=\varepsilon.
\]
To prove uniform convergence on $[0,1]\setminus E$, let $\delta>0$ be given and choose $k\in\mathbb N$ such that $1/k<\delta$. If $x\in[0,1]\setminus E$, then $x\notin A_{k,N_k}$, which means $f_n(x)\le 1/k$ for all $n\ge N_k$. Hence for all $n\ge N_k$,
\[
\label{eq:8.u111}
\sup_{x\in[0,1]\setminus E} f_n(x)\le 1/k<\delta.
\]
This is exactly uniform convergence of $f_n$ to $0$ on $[0,1]\setminus E$.
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 8.8

Theorem 8.5
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:8.5}
Since $\int_\Omega F<\infty$, one has $F(x)<\infty$ for almost every $x\in\Omega$; replacing $\Omega$ by the subset where $F<\infty$ (which changes neither integrals nor pointwise convergence almost everywhere) may assume $F(x)<\infty$ for all $x\in\Omega$. Then $f_n(x)\in\mathbb{R}$ for all $n$ and $x$, and the pointwise limit $f$ is measurable.

For each $x\in\Omega$, taking limits in $|f_n(x)|\le F(x)$ gives $|f(x)|\le F(x)$. Hence $\int_\Omega |f|\le \int_\Omega F<\infty$, so $f$ is absolutely integrable, and also $\int_\Omega |f_n|\le \int_\Omega F<\infty$ for all $n$.

The functions $F+f_n$ are nonnegative and converge pointwise to $F+f$. By Fatou's lemma,
\[
\label{eq:8.u133}
\int_\Omega (F+f)\le \liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega (F+f_n)=\int_\Omega F+\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega f_n,
\]
so $\int_\Omega f\le \liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega f_n$.

Similarly, $F-f_n\ge 0$ and $F-f_n\to F-f$ pointwise, so Fatou's lemma yields
\[
\label{eq:8.u134}
\int_\Omega (F-f)\le \liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega (F-f_n)=\int_\Omega F-\limsup_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega f_n,
\]
which is equivalent to $\int_\Omega f\ge \limsup_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega f_n$.

Therefore $\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega f_n\ge \int_\Omega f\ge \limsup_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega f_n$, so the limit exists and equals $\int_\Omega f$.
\end{proof}

label: Definition 8.11
Lemma 8.9
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:lem:8.9}
By assumption,
\[
\label{eq:8.u140}
\overline{\int}_{\Omega} f=\underline{\int}_{\Omega} f=A\in\mathbb{R},
\]
so $f$ is integrable over $\Omega$ and $\int_{\Omega} f:=A$.

To prove absolute integrability, use the pointwise identities
\[
\label{eq:8.u141}
|f|=\max\{f,-f\}=\frac{f+|f|}{2}+\frac{-f+|f|}{2}.
\]
Since $|f|\ge f$ and $|f|\ge -f$, monotonicity of the upper integral gives
\[
\label{eq:8.u142}
\overline{\int}_{\Omega}|f|\ge \overline{\int}_{\Omega} f = A,
\qquad
\overline{\int}_{\Omega}|f|\ge \overline{\int}_{\Omega}(-f).
\]
Also, from $\underline{\int}_{\Omega} f=A$ and the relation $\overline{\int}_{\Omega}(-f)=-\underline{\int}_{\Omega} f$ (which follows directly from the definitions by negating the class of majorants/minorants), it follows that
\[
\label{eq:8.u143}
\overline{\int}_{\Omega}(-f)=-A\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
Now $|f|\le f^+ + f^-$ with $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$ and $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $f=f^+-f^-$. Using the elementary bounds $0\le f^+\le |f|$ and $0\le f^-\le |f|$ and additivity of the integral for integrable functions, one obtains
\[
\label{eq:8.u144}
\int_{\Omega} f^+ = \frac{1}{2}\left(\int_{\Omega}|f|+\int_{\Omega} f\right),
\qquad
\int_{\Omega} f^- = \frac{1}{2}\left(\int_{\Omega}|f|-\int_{\Omega} f\right).
\]
In particular, finiteness of $\int_{\Omega} f$ and $\int_{\Omega}(-f)$ implies finiteness of both $\int_{\Omega} f^+$ and $\int_{\Omega} f^-$, hence
\[
\label{eq:8.u145}
\int_{\Omega}|f|=\int_{\Omega} f^+ + \int_{\Omega} f^- <\infty.
\]
Therefore $f$ is absolutely integrable, and the stated equalities for $\int_{\Omega} f$, $\overline{\int}_{\Omega} f$, and $\underline{\int}_{\Omega} f$ follow from the hypothesis.
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 8.11
Proposition 8.12
Proposition 8.13
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:8.13}
Since $f$ is Riemann integrable on the bounded interval $I$, it is bounded: there exists $M\ge 0$ such that $|f(x)|\le M$ for all $x\in I$. In particular, $\int_I |f|\,dx\le M\,m(I)<\infty$, so once measurability is known, $f\in L^1(I)$.

To prove measurability, define for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$ the oscillation at scale $1/n$ by
\[
\label{eq:8.u154}
\omega_n(x):=\sup\{f(y):y\in I,\ |y-x|<1/n\}-\inf\{f(y):y\in I,\ |y-x|<1/n\},\qquad x\in I.
\]
Each of the functions $x\mapsto \sup\{f(y):|y-x|<1/n\}$ and $x\mapsto \inf\{f(y):|y-x|<1/n\}$ is Borel measurable (as a pointwise supremum/infimum of translates of $f$ over open balls), hence $\omega_n$ is Borel measurable. Let
\[
\label{eq:8.u155}
D:=\{x\in I: f\text{ is discontinuous at }x\}.
\]
Then $x\in D$ if and only if $\lim_{n\to\infty}\omega_n(x)>0$. Consequently,
\[
\label{eq:8.u156}
D=\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty \bigcap_{N=1}^\infty \bigcup_{n\ge N}\{x\in I: \omega_n(x)\ge 1/k\},
\]
so $D$ is Borel measurable.

A standard characterization of Riemann integrability states that $f$ is Riemann integrable on $I$ if and only if the set $D$ of discontinuities has Lebesgue measure zero. Hence $m(D)=0$. Define $g:=f\,\mathbf{1}_{I\setminus D}$ on $I$. Then $g$ agrees with $f$ almost everywhere on $I$, and $g$ is continuous at every point of $I\setminus D$. In particular, $g$ is Borel measurable, so $f$ is Lebesgue measurable as it differs from $g$ only on the null set $D$.

Since $f$ is bounded and $m(I)<\infty$, it follows that $f\in L^1(I)$.

Finally, for each tagged partition $P$ of $I$ with mesh $\|P\|$, the Riemann sum $S(P,f)$ satisfies
\[
\label{eq:8.u157}
S(P,f)=\sum_{j} f(t_j)\,|I_j|.
\]
Let $L(P,f)$ and $U(P,f)$ denote the lower and upper Darboux sums. For every $P$ one has $L(P,f)\le S(P,f)\le U(P,f)$. Let $\underline{\int}_I f$ and $\overline{\int}_I f$ be the lower and upper Riemann integrals. Riemann integrability means $\underline{\int}_I f=\overline{\int}_I f=:R\cdot\int_I f$, and for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a partition $P$ with $U(P,f)-L(P,f)<\varepsilon$.

Let $\varepsilon>0$ and choose such a partition $P$. Since $f$ is measurable and bounded, the Lebesgue integral satisfies
\[
\label{eq:8.u158}
L(P,f)\le \int_I f\,dx\le U(P,f),
\]
because on each subinterval $I_j$ one has $\inf_{I_j} f\le f\le \sup_{I_j} f$ and integrating over $I_j$ gives $\inf_{I_j} f\,|I_j|\le \int_{I_j} f\,dx\le \sup_{I_j} f\,|I_j|$, then summing over $j$. Hence
\[
\label{eq:8.u159}
\bigl|\,\int_I f\,dx - R\cdot\int_I f\,\bigr|\le U(P,f)-L(P,f)<\varepsilon.
\]
Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, $\int_I f\,dx=R\cdot\int_I f$.
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 8.14
Theorem 8.6
content:
\begin{theorem}
\label{thm:8.6}
[Fubini--Tonelli for absolutely integrable functions on $\mathbb{R}^2$]
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ be Lebesgue measurable and assume
\[
\label{eq:8.u163}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} |f(x,y)|\,d(x,y) < \infty.
\]
Then, for almost every $x\in\mathbb{R}$ the function $y\mapsto f(x,y)$ is integrable on $\mathbb{R}$, and for almost every $y\in\mathbb{R}$ the function $x\mapsto f(x,y)$ is integrable on $\mathbb{R}$. The functions
\[
\label{eq:8.u164}
F(x):=\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x,y)\,dy,\qquad G(y):=\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x,y)\,dx
\]
are integrable on $\mathbb{R}$, and the following equalities hold:
\[
\label{eq:8.u165}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} f(x,y)\,d(x,y)
= \int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x,y)\,dy\right)dx
= \int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x,y)\,dx\right)dy.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\label{eq:8.u166}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} |f(x,y)|\,dy\right)dx
=\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} |f(x,y)|\,d(x,y)
=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} |f(x,y)|\,dx\right)dy.
\]
\end{theorem}
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:8.6}
Set $g(x,y)=|f(x,y)|$. Then $g\ge 0$ is measurable and $\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} g\,d(x,y)<\infty$.

Define $g_n(x,y):=\min\{g(x,y),n\}$ for $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Then $0\le g_n\uparrow g$ pointwise and each $g_n$ is measurable and bounded. For each $n$, Tonelli's theorem for nonnegative measurable functions gives
\[
\label{eq:8.u167}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} g_n\,d(x,y)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} g_n(x,y)\,dy\right)dx
=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} g_n(x,y)\,dx\right)dy.
\]
By the monotone convergence theorem, for almost every $x$,
\[
\label{eq:8.u168}
\int_{\mathbb{R}} g_n(x,y)\,dy \uparrow \int_{\mathbb{R}} g(x,y)\,dy \in [0,\infty],
\]
and similarly for almost every $y$ with the roles of $x$ and $y$ exchanged. Applying monotone convergence again to the outer integrals yields
\[
\label{eq:8.u169}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} g(x,y)\,dy\right)dx
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} g_n(x,y)\,dy\right)dx
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} g_n\,d(x,y)
=\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} g\,d(x,y)<\infty.
\]
In particular $x\mapsto \int_{\mathbb{R}} g(x,y)\,dy$ is integrable and finite almost everywhere. The same argument with the variables exchanged shows
\[
\label{eq:8.u170}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} g(x,y)\,dx\right)dy=\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} g\,d(x,y)<\infty.
\]
Thus for almost every $x$, $y\mapsto f(x,y)$ is absolutely integrable (since $\int |f(x,y)|\,dy<\infty$), and similarly for almost every $y$.

Now define $f^+(x,y)=\max\{f(x,y),0\}$ and $f^-(x,y)=\max\{-f(x,y),0\}$, so that $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^+ + f^-$. Since $\int |f|<\infty$, one has $\int f^+<\infty$ and $\int f^-<\infty$. Applying the already established nonnegative case to $f^+$ and $f^-$ gives
\[
\label{eq:8.u171}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} f^{\pm}\,d(x,y)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} f^{\pm}(x,y)\,dy\right)dx
=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} f^{\pm}(x,y)\,dx\right)dy.
\]
Subtracting the identities for $f^-$ from those for $f^+$ yields
\[
\label{eq:8.u172}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} f\,d(x,y)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x,y)\,dy\right)dx
=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x,y)\,dx\right)dy.
\]
The equalities for $|f|$ are the corresponding nonnegative statements already proved.
\end{proof}

label: Theorem 8.7
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:8.7}
Set $h(x,y):=|f(x,y)|$. Then $h\ge 0$ is measurable and $\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} h<\infty$.

By Tonelli's theorem for nonnegative functions, the functions
\[
\label{eq:8.u177}
H_1(x):=\int_{\mathbb{R}} h(x,y)\,dy,\qquad H_2(y):=\int_{\mathbb{R}} h(x,y)\,dx
\]
are measurable (possibly taking the value $+\infty$) and satisfy
\[
\label{eq:8.u178}
\int_{\mathbb{R}} H_1(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} h(x,y)\,dx\,dy=\int_{\mathbb{R}} H_2(y)\,dy<\infty.
\]
Hence $H_1(x)<\infty$ for almost every $x$, and $H_2(y)<\infty$ for almost every $y$.

If $H_1(x)<\infty$, then
\[
\label{eq:8.u179}
\int_{\mathbb{R}} |f(x,y)|\,dy=H_1(x)<\infty,
\]
so $y\mapsto f(x,y)$ is absolutely integrable and $F(x):=\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x,y)\,dy$ is a finite real number. Moreover, for such $x$,
\[
\label{eq:8.u180}
|F(x)|\le \int_{\mathbb{R}} |f(x,y)|\,dy=H_1(x).
\]
Therefore $|F|\le H_1$ almost everywhere, and thus
\[
\label{eq:8.u181}
\int_{\mathbb{R}} |F(x)|\,dx\le \int_{\mathbb{R}} H_1(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} |f(x,y)|\,dx\,dy<\infty,
\]
so $F\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$. The same argument with $H_2$ shows that for almost every $y$, $x\mapsto f(x,y)$ is absolutely integrable, $G(y):=\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x,y)\,dx$ is finite, and $G\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$.

To identify the integrals, write $f=f^+-f^-$ with $f^+,f^-\ge 0$ measurable and $|f|=f^++f^-$. Since $\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} |f|<\infty$, both $\int f^+$ and $\int f^-$ are finite. Applying Tonelli's theorem to $f^+$ and $f^-$ yields, for almost every $x$,
\[
\label{eq:8.u182}
\int_{\mathbb{R}} f^+(x,y)\,dy<\infty,\qquad \int_{\mathbb{R}} f^-(x,y)\,dy<\infty,
\]
and
\[
\label{eq:8.u183}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}\Big(\int_{\mathbb{R}} f^+(x,y)\,dy\Big)dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} f^+(x,y)\,dx\,dy,
\]
\[
\label{eq:8.u184}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}\Big(\int_{\mathbb{R}} f^-(x,y)\,dy\Big)dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} f^-(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
\]
For almost every $x$, linearity of the integral in $y$ gives
\[
\label{eq:8.u185}
F(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x,y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb{R}} f^+(x,y)\,dy-\int_{\mathbb{R}} f^-(x,y)\,dy.
\]
Integrating in $x$ and using the preceding equalities,
\[
\label{eq:8.u186}
\int_{\mathbb{R}} F(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} f^+(x,y)\,dx\,dy-\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} f^-(x,y)\,dx\,dy=\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} f(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
\]
The equality $\int_{\mathbb{R}} G(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} f(x,y)\,dx\,dy$ follows by the same argument with the roles of $x$ and $y$ interchanged.
\end{proof}
